groups.label: Let the representation do the talking
groups.summary: Problems in which the decisive move is to read, transform, or audit a graph, snapshot sequence, or other motion representation.
checks: The algebra is usually light; success depends on attaching the right physical meaning to slope, area, sign, spacing, and time interval.

groups.label: Close the journey bookkeeping
groups.summary: Travel problems solved by reconciling distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and elapsed time across one or more legs or movers.
checks: Make a compact journey ledger, decide what is closing or accumulating, and only then divide or equate.

groups.label: Choose the missing-link acceleration
groups.summary: Straight-line changing-motion problems where the main judgment is which constant-acceleration relation or time symmetry closes the data.
checks: List knowns with signs, identify the missing variable, and choose the one relation that avoids introducing another unknown.

groups.label: Separate the flight into axes
groups.summary: Projectile and release problems whose solution comes from sharing one clock between independent horizontal and vertical motion.
checks: Split the initial velocity, solve the vertical timing, and carry that same time into the horizontal story.

groups.label: Keep signs and directions honest
groups.summary: Qualitative and short quantitative problems where vector character, reversal, or the direction of acceleration is the actual test.
checks: Draw a positive direction or a local velocity arrow before calculating; the trap is nearly always a lost sign or confused magnitude.

atoms.label: Solve a meeting or synchronized-arrival condition for constant-speed movers
atoms.summary: Choose one clock and origin, write a position or travel-time expression for each mover, and impose the meeting or arrival condition.
checks: Two objects or signals leave at different times, move toward or away from one another, or arrive together.
atoms.classification_note: Determine an encounter, separation, delay, or simultaneous arrival by linking two uniform-motion timelines.

atoms.label: Reconstruct or compare a two-dimensional motion vector from components
atoms.summary: Establish common axes, relate the component ratio to the path angle, solve or compare components, and recombine them when a resultant is requested.
checks: x/y displacement components, a path angle and one velocity component, or horizontal and vertical velocity components that change differently.
atoms.classification_note: Recover or compare a resultant displacement or velocity direction/magnitude when perpendicular components, a path angle, or changes in components are given.

atoms.label: Classify motion quantities as scalar or vector and distinguish paired quantities
atoms.summary: Ask whether direction is essential to the definition, then keep magnitude-only and directed quantities separate.
checks: Asks whether distance, displacement, speed, velocity, or acceleration is scalar or vector.
atoms.classification_note: Identify which motion quantities require direction and distinguish related scalar-vector pairs.

atoms.label: Choose the valid slope, area, or ordinate operation on a motion graph
atoms.summary: Read both axes and units, test the candidate operation dimensionally, and distinguish a selector question from a quantitative slope or area task.
checks: A multiple-choice or conceptual prompt asks what a graph gradient, tangent, area, or ordinate represents.
atoms.classification_note: Audit which graph operation has the dimensions and physical meaning of the requested motion quantity, without yet carrying out a substantial area or tangent calculation.

atoms.label: Infer velocity and acceleration from equal-time position snapshots
atoms.summary: Compare successive spacings for speed, then compare how those spacings change for acceleration and direction.
checks: Dots or object positions are shown at successive equal time intervals.
atoms.classification_note: Infer velocity and acceleration behavior from positions recorded at equal time intervals.

atoms.label: Determine velocity change from area under an acceleration–time graph
atoms.summary: Use a(t)=F(t)/m when needed, integrate the signed area for Δv, then combine with the stated initial velocity.
checks: An acceleration–time trace is supplied, or a force–time trace and constant mass are supplied, and velocity change or final velocity is requested.
atoms.classification_note: Calculate a change in velocity, or a final velocity, from an acceleration–time trace or from a force–time trace after converting force to acceleration for known constant mass.

atoms.label: Determine instantaneous or average acceleration from a velocity–time trace
atoms.summary: Choose the relevant point or interval, form rise over run with signs and units, and use a tangent for a curved trace.
checks: A linear velocity- or speed-time trace is shown and acceleration at an instant or over an interval is requested.
atoms.classification_note: Determine instantaneous or interval linear acceleration from a velocity- or speed-time gradient or tangent.

atoms.label: Translate between position, velocity, acceleration, speed, and distance traces
atoms.summary: Translate through slopes, signed areas, turning points, and continuity rather than copying the source outline.
checks: One linear position-, displacement-, distance-, speed-, velocity-, or acceleration trace is supplied and another linear-motion trace must be inferred.
atoms.classification_note: Construct or select one linear-motion trace from another through a derivative, accumulated area, sign change, or turning point.

atoms.label: Distinguish zero instantaneous velocity from nonzero acceleration at a linear-motion turning point
atoms.summary: Set the relevant instantaneous velocity component to zero at the turn, then determine acceleration independently from the stated linear-motion model.
checks: A linear throw, rise, or rebound reaches a maximum height or reversal point and the question asks about instantaneous velocity or acceleration there.
atoms.classification_note: A vertically moving body or ideal projectile reaches a turning point while gravitational acceleration remains nonzero.

atoms.label: Infer zero acceleration from constant velocity
atoms.summary: Check both magnitude and direction of velocity; when neither changes, set acceleration to zero before any shared force or energy consequence.
checks: Velocity is constant in both magnitude and direction, or the body is at rest, and the demanded bridge is zero acceleration.
atoms.classification_note: Rest, hover, straight-line constant velocity, or a terminal-speed case shared with A.1.13.

atoms.label: Use velocity and acceleration directions to tell speeding up from slowing down
atoms.summary: Put velocity and acceleration on one signed axis; same direction means speeding up and opposite directions mean slowing down.
checks: The actual test is whether velocity magnitude rises or falls, not merely the sign of acceleration.
atoms.classification_note: A body moves along a line while velocity and acceleration directions or signs are stated, drawn, or inferred.

atoms.label: Recover an unknown motion-graph scale from a stated displacement or distance
atoms.summary: Partition the graph into simple regions, write their signed areas in terms of the unknown scale, and equate to the stated motion total.
checks: A velocity-time graph has a missing scale and the journey distance or displacement is supplied.
atoms.classification_note: Infer an unlabeled or unknown graph-axis value by making the total signed area match a stated displacement or distance.

atoms.label: Determine net displacement from signed area under a velocity–time graph
atoms.summary: Calculate each geometric area with its sign and add algebraically; use absolute areas only if distance is explicitly requested.
checks: The trace crosses the time axis, reverses direction, or asks for displacement rather than total distance.
atoms.classification_note: Calculate or compare net displacement from positive and negative regions under a velocity-time graph.

atoms.label: Determine distance from area under a speed–time graph
atoms.summary: Partition or estimate the area between the speed trace and the time axis and add every region positively.
checks: A speed–time trace is supplied and distance travelled is requested.
atoms.classification_note: Calculate total distance from the positive area under a speed–time graph, including an estimated curved area.

atoms.label: Distinguish path length from displacement and their corresponding average rates
atoms.summary: Sum the full path for distance and use the endpoint-change vector for displacement; divide each by the same elapsed time only when average rates are requested.
checks: A curved, turning, or returning journey asks for distance versus displacement directly, or supplies one elapsed time and asks for average speed versus average velocity.
atoms.classification_note: Compare or calculate the total path length and the endpoint displacement for a journey, including when those quantities feed average speed and average velocity.

atoms.label: Distinguish and determine instantaneous and average speed from a motion trace
atoms.summary: Use a tangent for the instant and a secant or journey total for the interval; compare like units and signs.
checks: Compares tangent gradient at one time with chord gradient or total distance divided by elapsed time.
atoms.classification_note: Distinguish the speed at an instant from a speed averaged over an interval, usually on a nonlinear position-time trace.

atoms.label: Determine a missing distance, time, or speed for one uniform leg
atoms.summary: Choose distance or displacement consistently, convert units, and use distance = speed × time for that one leg.
checks: One path length, one elapsed time, and one constant speed or velocity are linked directly.
atoms.classification_note: Find one missing distance, elapsed time, or speed for a single uniform leg, excluding a return/reflection condition.

atoms.label: Determine average speed over a multi-stage journey
atoms.summary: Sum the actual distances and sum all elapsed times separately, then divide total distance by total time.
checks: A journey has multiple distances, speeds, or time intervals and asks for one average.
atoms.classification_note: Find an overall average speed for unequal stages, stops, or return legs.

atoms.label: Determine average speed over one complete oscillation
atoms.summary: Trace the full cycle path as 4 × amplitude and divide by the period, or multiply by frequency.
checks: Average speed over a complete cycle is requested; the total path is nonzero even though net displacement is zero.
atoms.classification_note: A particle or medium point completes one oscillation with a stated amplitude and period or frequency.

atoms.label: Determine speed or distance from an ordinary round-trip signal transit
atoms.summary: Draw the outward and return legs, total the actual path, and match it to the relevant elapsed time or period.
checks: An ordinary echo, pulse reflection, or return journey supplies a doubled or partitioned path.
atoms.classification_note: Relate distance, time, and signal speed when a non-relativistic journey returns, reflects, or echoes.

atoms.label: Determine signed velocity change and average acceleration through a reversal
atoms.summary: Choose a positive direction, write one velocity negative, and subtract velocities rather than speed magnitudes.
checks: A bounce, rebound, reflection, or U-turn explicitly reverses the direction of motion.
atoms.classification_note: Calculate or reason about a genuine change of direction in which the final velocity has the opposite sign from the initial velocity.

atoms.label: Compare vertical motions with different initial velocities under the same uniform g
atoms.summary: Write separate signed vertical-motion equations with the correct inherited initial velocities and compare at a common time or height.
checks: Two falling objects share gravity but one is dropped, thrown, or released from a moving carrier.
atoms.classification_note: Compare fall times, speeds, or separations for bodies released or projected with different initial velocities under the same g.

atoms.label: Use endpoint mean speed to determine uniform-acceleration displacement
atoms.summary: Confirm constant acceleration, compute mean velocity as half the signed endpoint sum, and multiply by time.
checks: Initial velocity, final velocity, and time are given and distance or an average-power route needs the travelled distance.
atoms.classification_note: Find displacement during uniform acceleration from elapsed time and the mean of the endpoint velocities.

atoms.label: Use signed endpoint velocity change to determine acceleration, time, or final velocity
atoms.summary: Choose a positive direction, form final velocity minus initial velocity, and divide or rearrange using the elapsed time.
checks: Initial velocity, final velocity, and time or acceleration are linked directly.
atoms.classification_note: Find an average or constant acceleration, an elapsed time, or an endpoint velocity from signed velocity change over time.

atoms.label: Solve a meeting condition by cancelling a shared uniform acceleration
atoms.summary: Write both positions on one axis, equate them, cancel the common acceleration term, and solve the remaining relative-motion relation.
checks: Two bodies start together in time, have different initial positions or velocities, and share the same gravitational acceleration.
atoms.classification_note: Find when two bodies meet by subtracting position equations whose identical acceleration terms cancel.

atoms.label: Find when a uniformly accelerating pursuer catches a constant-speed leader
atoms.summary: Write both displacements from the shared event, equate vt to ½at² (or the applicable uniformly accelerated form), discard the trivial t=0 root, and solve the remaining factor.
checks: One traveller passes another at constant speed exactly when the second starts from rest with constant acceleration, and a catch time or position is requested.
atoms.classification_note: Find the nonzero catch time when a uniformly accelerating pursuer and a constant-speed leader share the same start event and later position.

atoms.label: Determine displacement during a specified second of uniform acceleration
atoms.summary: Calculate cumulative displacement to the two interval boundaries and subtract, or use the derived nth-interval expression.
checks: Asks for distance travelled during the nth second rather than during the first n seconds.
atoms.classification_note: Find the displacement during one specified one-second interval of uniformly accelerated motion.

atoms.label: Determine g from measured fall distance and time
atoms.summary: Use the stated initial conditions in s=ut+½at², set a=g, and rearrange for g; keep any uncertainty propagation as a separate shared operation.
checks: A drop experiment supplies a measured fall distance and time and asks for g.
atoms.classification_note: Infer gravitational acceleration from a measured vertical distance and fall time; uncertainty may appear as a shared data-analysis extension.

atoms.label: Determine displacement after a known time under uniform acceleration
atoms.summary: Use signed s=ut+½at²; for rest cases use s=½at² bidirectionally so smaller acceleration at fixed displacement implies longer time.
checks: Uniform acceleration and time are supplied for a displacement calculation, or fixed displacement from rest is compared under different accelerations.
atoms.classification_note: Connect displacement, uniform acceleration, and elapsed time, including finding displacement from time and inverse qualitative reasoning from rest at fixed displacement.

atoms.label: Use v²=u²+2as when time is absent
atoms.summary: Choose signs, use final-speed squared = initial-speed squared + twice acceleration times displacement, and interpret the physical root.
checks: Stopping distance, braking, launch length, or a speed after a known displacement with uniform acceleration.
atoms.classification_note: Link speed change, acceleration, and displacement when elapsed time is absent or deliberately unnecessary.

atoms.label: Determine free-fall speed from vertical drop height
atoms.summary: Set the initial vertical velocity and sign convention, apply the no-time relation, and select the positive speed magnitude if asked.
checks: Drop height and impact speed, or an equivalent free-fall distance comparison, under constant g.
atoms.classification_note: Relate vertical distance and speed for free fall, usually from rest, without needing the fall time.

atoms.label: Sketch or select a motion trace from a linear-motion story
atoms.summary: Divide the story into phases; set signs and continuity; encode each phase through slope, curvature, and acceleration.
checks: The stem narrates phases of linear motion and asks for a position-, velocity-, speed-, or acceleration-time trace.
atoms.classification_note: A straight-line journey with accelerating, constant-speed, stopping, or reversal phases is described in words.

atoms.label: Track how acceleration magnitude changes during non-uniform motion
atoms.summary: Identify the changing quantity, infer the corresponding net-acceleration trend, then translate that trend into velocity or graph curvature.
checks: The question asks how velocity or acceleration evolves when the net influence varies continuously.
atoms.classification_note: A driving or resisting influence changes with speed, position, mass, or time, so the acceleration is not constant.

atoms.label: Represent successive stages of uniform and non-uniform acceleration
atoms.summary: List the stages in time order, determine acceleration sign and behavior in each, and join the trace with physically valid continuity.
checks: A stage boundary changes acceleration and the resulting motion or trace must be compared across stages.
atoms.classification_note: Motion passes through distinct acceleration stages before, during, or after a change in conditions.

atoms.label: Recognize uniformly accelerated motion from a stated uniform field
atoms.summary: Translate uniform field to constant force to constant acceleration, then infer the motion description.
checks: Uniform electric or gravitational field, constant field strength, constant force on fixed mass, or a choice between uniform and uniformly accelerated linear motion.
atoms.classification_note: Infer constant acceleration and uniformly accelerated one-dimensional motion when a fixed-mass particle moves in a spatially uniform field.

atoms.label: Use ideal vertical-flight timing and velocity symmetry
atoms.summary: Take upward as positive, use zero vertical velocity at the apex, and double the one-way time only when start and finish heights match.
checks: An object is projected vertically and returns to its launch level or reaches an apex.
atoms.classification_note: Use constant gravitational acceleration and equal-height symmetry to connect ascent time, descent time, launch speed, or return speed.

atoms.label: Test whether an ideal projectile clears a stated height
atoms.summary: Resolve the launch velocity, obtain time from horizontal motion, and evaluate vertical displacement at that same time.
checks: A ball or object follows a projectile path toward an obstacle, target, window, or rim.
atoms.classification_note: Determine whether a projectile reaches or clears a specified height at a known horizontal position or time.

atoms.label: Solve time, range, or impact velocity for a horizontal launch
atoms.summary: Solve vertical free fall for time, carry that time into horizontal motion, and combine impact components if required.
checks: Initial vertical velocity is zero while a horizontal speed and drop height are given.
atoms.classification_note: Find fall time, range, or impact velocity for an object launched horizontally from a height.

atoms.label: Determine velocity and acceleration at the apex of an ideal projectile
atoms.summary: Set only the vertical velocity component to zero; retain the horizontal component and downward gravitational acceleration.
checks: Asks about the apex, maximum height, or top of a projectile path with air resistance neglected.
atoms.classification_note: Identify or calculate velocity and acceleration at the highest point of ideal projectile motion.

atoms.label: Compare ideal-projectile ranges after inferring launch speed
atoms.summary: Translate the shared condition into a launch-speed ratio, then combine with the projectile range dependence under the stated angle and height.
checks: Two projectiles have different masses or launch conditions but an equal non-kinematic quantity, then their ranges are compared.
atoms.classification_note: Compare ranges for projectiles whose launch speeds must first be inferred from energy, momentum, or another shared condition.

atoms.label: Predict ideal projectile motion after release with a stated tangent velocity
atoms.summary: Take the release velocity tangent to the circle, resolve its components, and then use projectile motion from the release point.
checks: A string breaks, contact is lost, or a particle is released from a rotating or circular system.
atoms.classification_note: Determine the subsequent projectile path or landing point when an object leaves a circular path.

atoms.label: Track horizontal and vertical velocity components during ideal projectile motion
atoms.summary: Resolve the launch velocity; keep the horizontal component constant when drag is absent; evolve the vertical component linearly under g with its sign.
checks: The question compares Vh and Vv, asks for component graphs, or follows a projectile before or after its apex.
atoms.classification_note: Determine or graph how the horizontal and vertical components of projectile velocity change during a specified flight segment.

atoms.label: Recombine ideal-projectile velocity components at impact
atoms.summary: Retain the horizontal component, obtain the impact vertical component kinematically, and combine the perpendicular components.
checks: The impact speed or direction is requested and the official route requires horizontal and vertical velocity components.
atoms.classification_note: Determine resultant speed or direction at impact by finding and recombining perpendicular projectile velocity components.

atoms.label: Recognize the parabolic path produced by ideal projectile components
atoms.summary: Resolve motion parallel and perpendicular to the acceleration; eliminate the common time between uniform and accelerated components.
checks: A particle enters a uniform field with velocity not parallel to the field, and its path shape is requested.
atoms.classification_note: Identify the path produced by constant acceleration along one axis and uniform motion along the perpendicular axis.

atoms.label: Recombine horizontal and vertical projectile displacements
atoms.summary: Use the common flight time for both axes, then combine the perpendicular displacement components vectorially.
checks: Horizontal travel and vertical drop are known or calculable and the magnitude or direction of total displacement is asked.
atoms.classification_note: Find a projectile’s resultant displacement from independently accumulated horizontal and vertical displacements.

atoms.label: Compare ideal-projectile range and peak height when g changes
atoms.summary: Use the inverse-g dependence of both ideal range and maximum height at fixed launch conditions.
checks: The same launch is repeated on another planet or under a different g and both range and height are compared.
atoms.classification_note: Compare projectile range and peak height when launch speed and angle stay fixed but gravitational acceleration changes.

atoms.label: Solve an oblique ideal projectile that lands at a different height
atoms.summary: Resolve initial velocity, solve the vertical equation for the positive flight time, then use horizontal motion for range.
checks: Launch from a cliff or platform, landing above or below launch level, horizontal distance to impact, or a data-sufficiency question involving horizontal velocity, angle, and height.
atoms.classification_note: Determine horizontal range, or the information needed to determine it, when an obliquely launched projectile lands at a different vertical level.

atoms.label: Sketch or select a falling-motion trace with fluid resistance
atoms.summary: Track the velocity direction, compare drag with weight qualitatively, and make acceleration tend toward zero as terminal speed is approached.
checks: Fluid resistance or terminal speed is explicit and a qualitative speed, velocity, or acceleration trace is requested.
atoms.classification_note: A parachutist, raindrop, or other falling body accelerates through a fluid and may pass through distinct drag stages.

atoms.label: Relate velocity and acceleration directions during resisted falling motion
atoms.summary: Keep the current velocity direction separate from the net-force/acceleration direction and track the approach to the new terminal speed.
checks: The body is still moving downward while its acceleration may point upward.
atoms.classification_note: A skydiver or falling body changes from one terminal speed toward another after drag changes.

atoms.label: Explain or compare changing acceleration under fluid resistance
atoms.summary: Compare drag with weight qualitatively, update the net acceleration as speed changes, and identify the terminal condition when acceleration becomes zero.
checks: The demand concerns terminal-speed approach, acceleration magnitude, or a qualitative departure from the no-drag trajectory.
atoms.classification_note: A falling object or projectile moves through a gas or liquid while drag changes with speed.

atoms.label: Build a stagewise speed trace for a fall with changing fluid resistance
atoms.summary: Track the direction of motion, the drag change at each transition, the sign of acceleration, and each asymptotic terminal-speed section.
checks: The resisted fall has distinct stages and the complete qualitative speed-time trace is requested.
atoms.classification_note: A parachutist falls, reaches or approaches terminal speed, changes area, and approaches a new terminal speed.

atoms.label: Compare an actual resisted projectile trajectory with the ideal path
atoms.summary: Treat drag as opposite the instantaneous velocity and combine it qualitatively with weight to infer the lower, asymmetric path and altered impact direction; do not perform a quantitative two-dimensional drag calculation.
checks: A no-drag projectile path or impact direction is shown and the question asks how air resistance changes the peak, trajectory, or impact direction.
atoms.classification_note: Compare otherwise identical projectile motion with and without air resistance, qualitatively.

teaching_taxonomy.title: A1 Kinematics: question types and subtypes
teaching_taxonomy.scope: IB Physics, first assessment 2025; A.1 is common to SL and HL. K-codes below are report identifiers, not IB syllabus codes.
teaching_taxonomy.evidence_note: Examples establish the question type. The subtype lists also include directly implied syllabus variants; they are not claims that every variant has a separate past-paper occurrence. O = PACKET_007B_A1 taxonomy; N = PACKET_007B_A1_second taxonomy. These references are always version-qualified because their A1 codes differ.

families.name: Motion quantities, directions and averages
families.summary: Identify the quantity and the interval before calculating. Distinguish position, displacement, distance, speed, velocity and acceleration.

families.name: Motion graphs and position records
families.summary: Read, calculate from, construct and translate representations. Keep gradients, signed areas and graph heights separate.

families.name: Straight-line constant acceleration
families.summary: Choose a valid model, equation, time interval and boundary condition. Includes braking, staged journeys and scaling.

families.name: Vertical motion under gravity
families.summary: Treat g as a signed constant and choose the correct initial velocity. Includes upward throws, return times and release from moving objects.

families.name: Two-object timing and separation
families.summary: Use a shared origin and clock to compare positions, encounters and arrivals. These are same-frame kinematics applications.

families.name: Ideal projectile motion
families.summary: Resolve the launch, use a common flight time for independent axes, and recombine only when needed.

families.name: Fluid resistance and terminal motion
families.summary: Explain and sketch how drag changes motion. Current A.1 treatment is qualitative; force-law calculations add A.2.

families.name: Measurements, experiments and data analysis
families.summary: Extract motion from real measurements, handle geometry and uncertainty, and test a model. Includes current Paper 1B skills.

types.type: Define and distinguish motion quantities
subtypes: Position relative to a stated origin; displacement as final minus initial position
Distance and speed as scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration as vectors
Velocity and acceleration as rates of change
types.route: Choose the origin, direction, quantity and units before using an equation.
types.examples: O A1.3a, A1.4c, A1.5i; N A1.1c
types.boundary: The position/displacement distinction is explicit in the current syllabus, even where older questions use displacement loosely.

types.type: Compare distance, displacement and their average rates
subtypes: Out-and-back or multi-leg travel: total path versus endpoint displacement
Average speed versus average velocity
Perpendicular legs: find resultant displacement before average velocity
A complete return journey: zero average velocity with nonzero average speed
Curved path: arc length for distance versus chord/endpoints for displacement
types.route: Add path lengths for distance; subtract endpoint positions for displacement; divide each by the full elapsed time.
types.examples: Pack A Q6; Pack B Q40; O A1.4a–b; N A1.4b
types.boundary: An oscillation can supply the journey, but SHM-specific relations belong to C.1.

types.type: Distinguish instantaneous and interval-average values
subtypes: Read a value at one time versus calculate an average over an interval
Tangent gradient versus secant gradient
Locate a point at which instantaneous speed equals a stated average
types.route: Identify the time interval. Use a local rate for an instant and a total change divided by elapsed time for an average.
types.examples: Pack A Q5, Q28; O A1.5a–b; N A1.5a
types.boundary: A mean of endpoint speeds is not a general formula for average speed.

types.type: Interpret signs and directions of velocity and acceleration
subtypes: Positive or negative velocity as direction of travel
Same-sign velocity and acceleration: speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down in one dimension
Zero velocity at a turning point with nonzero acceleration
Constant velocity implies zero acceleration; constant speed on a curved path does not
types.route: Compare the directions of velocity and acceleration rather than treating negative acceleration as a synonym for slowing down.
types.examples: Pack A Q15, Q17; O A1.4d; N A1.2f–h
types.boundary: A quantitative centripetal-acceleration question belongs to A.2.

types.type: Resolve or reconstruct a motion vector
subtypes: Find perpendicular components from magnitude and angle
Recover a missing component from a path slope or component ratio
Recombine components into magnitude and direction
types.route: Use a consistent pair of axes, then trigonometry and vector addition.
types.examples: Pack A Q42(b); N A1.1b
types.boundary: Formal transformations between moving reference frames are A.5 HL, not a separate current A.1 requirement.

types.type: Solve uniform-speed journey and transit problems
subtypes: Find distance, time or speed for one leg
Combine legs, pauses or unequal-speed intervals
Echo/round-trip travel with the correct doubled distance
Infer pattern speed from a shift or spatial spacing and timing
types.route: Account for the actual travelled distance and total elapsed time, using s = vt for each uniform leg.
types.examples: O A1.1a–c, A1.1f, A1.1h–i; N A1.5b–e
types.boundary: Wave, optical or relativistic contexts may require additional topic knowledge. A fixed timing offset and a changed speed have different graph effects.

types.type: Calculate a velocity change and average acceleration through a direction change
subtypes: Opposite velocities before and after a rebound or reversal
Same speed with a changed direction
Vector subtraction for a two-dimensional velocity change
types.route: Calculate Δv = v_final − v_initial as a signed quantity or vector, then divide by the elapsed time.
types.examples: O A1.2k, A1.5c; N A1.5f
types.boundary: Subtracting the speed magnitudes can miss a nonzero velocity change. Inferring force or impulse adds A.2.

types.type: Identify the meaning of a graph feature
subtypes: Select the physical meaning of height, gradient, tangent or area
Match units to the requested operation
Reject a position–time area as a standard A.1 displacement, velocity or acceleration
Identify what an acceleration graph alone can and cannot determine
types.route: Read both axes and use dimensions plus the rate/accumulation relationships.
types.examples: Pack A Q18, Q32, Q44; O A1.2h; N A1.2a
types.boundary: Area under acceleration–time gives velocity change; an initial velocity is needed for the final velocity.

types.type: Calculate velocity or acceleration from a gradient
subtypes: Straight-line position–time gradient for velocity
Straight-line velocity–time gradient for acceleration
Tangent to a curved trace for an instantaneous rate
Secant across an interval for an average rate
types.route: Choose the correct line or tangent, use a sufficiently large rise/run triangle, and retain signs and units.
types.examples: Pack B Q38, Q46; O A1.2d–e; N A1.2d
types.boundary: A speed–time gradient describes the change in speed; signed vector acceleration requires the direction of motion.

types.type: Calculate displacement or distance from motion-graph area
subtypes: Signed velocity–time area for net displacement
Speed–time area for total distance
Split a velocity graph at zero and add absolute areas for distance
Handle a rebound or reversal without losing the area signs
Estimate area under a curved trace using a suitable graphical approximation
types.route: Add signed or absolute areas as required. Use simple regions or a justified estimate for a curved trace.
types.examples: Pack A Q33 / Pack B Q9; O A1.2b–c; N A1.3b, A1.4a; Pack B Q34(a)
types.boundary: The A33/B9 diagram includes a velocity jump at a rebound; it is not just one smooth upward flight.

types.type: Calculate velocity change from an acceleration history
subtypes: Positive, negative or mixed acceleration–time areas
Piecewise or nonuniform acceleration with a supplied graph
Find final velocity by adding the initial velocity
Convert a net-force graph to acceleration when mass is supplied
types.route: Find the signed area for Δv, then use v = u + Δv if an endpoint velocity is requested.
types.examples: Pack A Q12, Q41, Q44; O A1.2a; N A1.2c
types.boundary: Force-to-acceleration conversion adds A.2. Nonuniform graph work does not require a general calculus treatment.

types.type: Translate between motion representations
subtypes: Position–time to velocity–time, or velocity–time to acceleration–time
Velocity/speed trace to displacement/distance trace
Translate a turning point or rebound
Use slope, curvature and continuity rather than copying the outline
types.route: Translate rates and accumulated changes interval by interval, using the given initial conditions.
types.examples: Pack A Q1, Q37; Pack B Q46; O A1.2f, A1.2j; N A1.2e
types.boundary: Position normally stays continuous through an idealized rebound while velocity can jump.

types.type: Construct or describe a motion graph from a story
subtypes: Rest, uniform motion, uniform acceleration and nonuniform acceleration
Successive stages with changing motion
Read a graph back into a physical description
Distinguish changing acceleration magnitude from changing velocity
types.route: Mark the physical events, then set the sign, gradient and curvature for each interval.
types.examples: Pack A Q8(b); N A1.11a–c; O A1.11f
types.boundary: Resisted fall is developed separately in K7; construction is a skill distinct from selecting an MCQ graph.

types.type: Recover missing information or test graph sufficiency
subtypes: Unknown axis scale from a stated distance or displacement
Unknown time or peak speed from an area total
Recognize that endpoint velocities do not determine the full acceleration history
Explain why initial conditions are needed to reconstruct another trace
types.route: Write the known total as a graph area or rate relationship and identify which information remains unconstrained.
types.examples: O A1.2g, A1.11c; N A1.3a
types.boundary: Do not infer constant acceleration solely from two endpoint velocities.

types.type: Infer motion from equally timed position records
subtypes: Constant, increasing or decreasing spacing
Uniform versus nonuniform acceleration
Estimate speed from successive positions
Calculate acceleration from the change in interval speeds
types.route: Count time intervals correctly, compare spacings, and then compare changes in spacing.
types.examples: Pack A Q27, Q31; O A1.5h; N A1.2b
types.boundary: Experimental determination and uncertainty of g are developed in K8.

types.type: Select and justify the constant-acceleration model
subtypes: State the condition for using SUVAT equations
Identify given, hidden and unknown quantities
Recognize uniform acceleration from a constant gravitational or electric force under the stated assumptions
Judge a short-interval constant-acceleration approximation
types.route: Establish whether acceleration is constant over the interval, then select the equation that connects the available quantities.
types.boundary: Uniform gravitational/electric field examples may add D-topic knowledge. A uniform magnetic field does not generally produce constant vector acceleration. Varying drag invalidates one constant-a model for the full flight.

types.type: Solve a single interval of uniform acceleration
subtypes: Use v = u + at for endpoint velocity, acceleration or time
Use s = (u + v)t/2 for displacement
Use s = ut + at²/2 for displacement or time
Use v² = u² + 2as when time is absent
types.route: Set a positive direction, use signed quantities and solve the selected equation. Interpret any roots physically.
types.examples: Pack A Q19, Q22, Q42(a); N A1.7a, A1.8a, A1.9e, A1.10a
types.boundary: The four equations are solving routes within one broad type, with different known/unknown combinations.

types.type: Find a stopping distance or test a stopping boundary
subtypes: Time or distance to rest
Does a body reach a target before stopping?
Maximum permitted initial speed or minimum required deceleration
Compare braking distances when speed or deceleration changes
types.route: Use v = 0 at the stopping point, then compare the result with the available distance or time.
types.examples: Pack A Q22, Q35(a); O A1.10b–c
types.boundary: Deriving the deceleration from friction or forces adds A.2.

types.type: Join stages of a journey
subtypes: Accelerate, travel at constant speed, then decelerate
Reaction distance followed by braking distance
Different accelerations in successive intervals
Use one stage's final velocity as the next stage's initial velocity
types.route: Give each stage its own interval and model, carry boundary values forward, then add distances and times.
types.examples: Pack B Q41(a,c); O A1.6c; N A1.11c
types.boundary: Reaction time is a supplied modelling parameter; do not assume every stopping-distance item has a reaction stage.

types.type: Find travel during a specified interval or named second
subtypes: Distance during the nth second
Distances in successive equal time intervals
Reconstruct acceleration from a spacing pattern
Distinguish distance during an interval from distance since release
types.route: Evaluate positions at both ends of the requested interval and subtract; split again if direction reverses.
types.examples: Pack A Q13, Q36; O A1.9a, A1.10d; N A1.9c
types.boundary: An interval ending at 4 s is not automatically the fourth second.

types.type: Use kinematic scaling or a non-time graph
subtypes: From rest: displacement proportional to time squared
Speed proportional to the square root of displacement under fixed acceleration
Linear v²–s relations and their gradients
Ratio comparisons that avoid full numerical substitution
types.route: Rearrange the relevant kinematic relation into the variables shown, keeping fixed quantities explicit.
types.examples: Pack A Q24; O A1.10e; N A1.10a
types.boundary: Graph linearisation is also an experimental skill; a v–s gradient is not itself acceleration.

types.type: Calculate a drop or downward launch
subtypes: Released from rest
Thrown down with a nonzero initial velocity
Find fall time, height or impact speed
Compare results with a stated g
types.route: Use a consistent sign for g and the true initial velocity in the uniform-acceleration equations.
types.examples: Pack A Q2, Q16; N A1.10b
types.boundary: Free fall here means negligible resistance and approximately uniform g.

types.type: Calculate an upward vertical launch
subtypes: Time to the highest point and maximum rise
Return time to the launch level
Velocity or height during ascent and descent
Decide whether a specified height is reached
Launch upward from an elevated point and land below it: maximum rise versus absolute height, and full flight time
types.route: At the apex use v = 0 while retaining a = −g if upward is positive. Choose the correct branch of the motion.
types.examples: Pack A Q38; Pack B Q35(a–b); 2025 May SL P1A TZ2 Q1; O A1.9c, A1.10a; N A1.12a
types.boundary: Apex acceleration is not zero. Equal-height symmetry requires the ideal model.

types.type: Exploit two passage times or equal-height symmetry
subtypes: Infer launch speed from ascent and descent passage times at one height
Find the apex time as the midpoint of those passage times
Compare equal-height speeds and opposite velocity directions
types.route: Use the symmetry of ideal vertical motion, or solve the same height equation for its two times.
types.examples: Pack A Q26 / Pack B Q1; O A1.9b; N A1.12a
types.boundary: Different launch and landing heights do not have a return-time symmetry about the whole flight.

types.type: Release an object from a moving carrier
subtypes: Drop from a balloon rising at constant velocity
Compare release from a stationary and a moving carrier
Allow the released body to rise further before falling
Find the later ground impact using the inherited initial velocity
types.route: Give the body the carrier's instantaneous velocity at release, then evolve its free motion.
types.examples: Pack A Q11, Q34; N A1.6a
types.boundary: The word dropped does not imply zero ground-frame initial velocity.

types.type: Compare related ideal vertical motions
subtypes: Different initial speeds or upward/downward release directions
Same height and same speed magnitude with opposite launch directions
Different masses under the same g
Identify which of time, maximum height, impact speed and acceleration changes
types.route: Separate the initial conditions from the common acceleration, then compare the relevant equation or invariant.
types.examples: Pack A Q34; O A1.11e; N A1.6a
types.boundary: Only compare under the stated assumptions; drag can remove mass-independent motion.

types.type: Coordinate constant-speed encounters or arrivals
subtypes: Moving toward one another or in the same direction
Delayed starts and simultaneous arrivals
Two signal speeds with an arrival-time difference
A signal catching a moving receiver
types.route: Use one origin and clock; write a position or travel-time relation for each object and impose the stated encounter or arrival condition.
types.examples: O A1.1d–e, A1.1g; N A1.1a
types.boundary: This is same-frame algebra. Relativistic corrections or a formal change of frame add A.5 HL.

types.type: Find when an accelerating pursuer catches a leader
subtypes: An accelerating object pursuing a constant-speed object
Initial separation or a delayed start
Find meeting time and position
Reject the trivial shared starting-time root
types.route: Set the two positions equal using a common clock, solve, and retain the root corresponding to the requested later meeting.
types.examples: Pack B Q29; N A1.9b; O A1.9d
types.boundary: The initial separation must be included; equal velocities alone do not establish an encounter.

types.type: Find separation from two motion graphs
subtypes: Difference between two signed velocity–time areas
Include an initial separation
Recognize that equal velocities do not mean equal positions
Position–time graphs: intersections give meetings, and equal gradients give equal velocities
types.route: Find each change in position, add its initial position, and subtract the final positions.
types.examples: Pack A Q10; O A1.2i
types.boundary: Area between curves gives change in signed separation; its interpretation depends on initial positions.

types.type: Compare two bodies sharing the same acceleration
subtypes: Simultaneous motions with different initial velocities
One falling body released later than another
Increasing separation even after both have acceleration g
A meeting condition in which the common acceleration cancels
types.route: Write both position equations using the correct start times. Cancel the common acceleration only on an interval where both actually share it.
types.examples: Pack B Q45; O A1.11b; N A1.9a
types.boundary: The cancellation does not erase the first body's head start or the velocity it has gained.

types.type: Set up the projectile components and judge data sufficiency
subtypes: Horizontal, above-horizontal and below-horizontal launch
Resolve the initial velocity
Identify constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration
Decide which given quantities are needed for a requested range or time
Angles measured from the horizontal or from the vertical: choose sine/cosine accordingly
types.route: Choose axes, set ux and uy with signs, and use the same elapsed time in both directions.
types.examples: Pack A Q14, Q45; O A1.12a–c; Pack B Q28
types.boundary: The diagram in A45 shows launch 7° below horizontal; its text extraction alone is ambiguous.

types.type: Solve a horizontal launch
subtypes: Fall time from height
Range from horizontal speed and fall time
Infer launch speed or height from range and time
Compare linear horizontal and quadratic vertical time scaling
types.route: Solve the vertical fall first where useful, then use x = ux t.
types.examples: Pack A Q8(a), Q20, Q21, Q39; N A1.12c; O A1.12i
types.boundary: Horizontal speed does not alter fall time when height and initial vertical velocity are the same in the ideal model.

types.type: Solve an angled launch returning to the launch height
subtypes: Time of flight, range and maximum height
Find a launch component, speed or angle from supplied conditions
Use equal-height symmetry
Compare equal-speed launches at different angles
types.route: Resolve the launch and use the return condition y = 0. Any range shortcut must satisfy its equal-height assumptions.
types.examples: Pack B Q28, Q48; O A1.12l–n; N A1.12g, A1.12k; current syllabus; 2025 Nov SL P1A TZ1 Q2
types.boundary: Some inverse or angle-comparison variants are direct syllabus applications rather than individually verified examples in the packs.

types.type: Solve an angled launch ending at a different height
subtypes: Launch from a cliff or raised platform
Launch above or below the horizontal
Find flight time and horizontal range
Select the physically valid time from a quadratic
types.route: Use the actual signed vertical displacement in y = uy t − gt²/2, then find the horizontal motion.
types.examples: Pack A Q45; current syllabus; N A1.12l supports the related data-sufficiency question
types.boundary: The equal-launch/landing-height range formula does not apply unchanged.

types.type: Test clearance of a wall, net or target
subtypes: Height at a specified horizontal distance
Clearance margin versus an obstacle height
Whether the object hits an obstacle
Infer a limiting launch condition for clearance
types.route: Use the horizontal position to find the time, calculate vertical position at that same time, and compare like height references.
types.examples: Pack A Q8(c), Q9(a–b), Q45(bi–ii); N A1.12b
types.boundary: Account for whether distances refer to the object's centre, edge or bottom if the question makes that distinction.

types.type: Interpret the ideal path and apex
subtypes: Parabolic trajectory from uniform horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion
Constant horizontal velocity throughout flight
Zero vertical velocity at the apex but nonzero horizontal velocity
Downward acceleration at every point, including the apex
types.route: Apply the two component rules at the requested point instead of reasoning from the overall path shape alone.
types.examples: Pack A Q17, Q23; Pack B Q51; N A1.12d, A1.12g, A1.12i
types.boundary: A23 is ideal motion; the similar-looking A25 diagram is resisted motion and belongs in K7.

types.type: Find velocity, speed, direction or displacement during flight
subtypes: Components at a specified time or impact
Recombine velocity into speed and direction
Equal-height velocity comparison: only the vertical component reverses
Recombine perpendicular displacement components when resultant displacement is requested
types.route: Calculate the two components first, then use the magnitude and angle appropriate to the requested vector.
types.examples: Pack A Q45(biii); O A1.12f, A1.12m; N A1.12h, A1.12j
types.boundary: Speed, vertical velocity and resultant velocity are different requested outputs.

types.type: Compare related projectiles
subtypes: Common fall time but different horizontal speeds
Same initial velocity with different masses
Same momentum with different masses, so different launch speeds
Infer launch speed from a preceding energy or momentum condition
Compare range and maximum height when g changes
Equal-speed launches from the same height in different directions: different flight times but equal impact speeds at a common lower level, with negligible drag
types.route: Identify what is actually held constant, infer any hidden launch speeds, then compare vertical timing and horizontal travel.
types.examples: Pack A Q29 / Pack B Q4, Pack B Q39; N A1.12e, A1.12k; 2025 May SL P1A TZ3 Q2
types.boundary: The equal-momentum example is 2018 May SL P1 TZ2 Q9 and adds A.2; energy prerequisites add A.3. Same momentum is not the same condition as same velocity.

types.type: Predict motion after release or component-changing impact
subtypes: Release with the carrier's instantaneous velocity
Release from circular motion along the tangent, followed by projectile flight
Compare outgoing angles after different changes to horizontal and vertical components
types.route: Establish the initial or outgoing velocity at the event, then apply the independent projectile-component rules.
types.boundary: Circular-force reasoning and the mechanism of a bounce belong to A.2; the subsequent flight can independently be A.1.

types.type: Explain terminal speed and the approach to it
subtypes: Speed increases while acceleration decreases
Terminal motion has constant velocity and zero acceleration
Explain the qualitative effect of increasing resistance
Distinguish zero resultant force from no forces acting
types.route: Link the changing speed to resistance and the resulting change in acceleration until steady motion is reached.
types.examples: Pack A Q30, Q43; O A1.13i; N A1.13c
types.boundary: The force-balance calculations in A30/A43 are A.2 overlap; qualitative terminal motion is A.1.

types.type: Recognize or draw resisted-motion graphs
subtypes: Speed–time approach to a horizontal asymptote
Position–time approaching a constant gradient
Acceleration–time approaching zero
Acceleration–speed relation and terminal intercept
Compare terminal-speed curves for different bodies qualitatively
types.route: Use the stated sign convention and the conditions for initial motion and terminal motion to constrain the curve.
types.examples: O A1.13a–c, A1.13e; N A1.13a; 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ3 Q1(e)
types.boundary: Do not assign an exact curve or terminal-speed ratio from mass/size alone without a specified resistance model.

types.type: Follow a change in resistance or parachute opening
subtypes: Initial acceleration toward one terminal speed
Sudden increase in drag
Downward velocity with upward acceleration while slowing
Approach to a new lower terminal speed
Stagewise speed or velocity sketches
types.route: Preserve the direction of travel, change the acceleration when resistance changes, and connect the stages to the new steady state.
types.examples: Pack A Q15; O A1.13c–d; N A1.13b, A1.13d
types.boundary: Velocity does not instantaneously reverse when a parachute opens.

types.type: Compare acceleration and components in resisted flight
subtypes: Drag opposing the velocity on ascent and descent
Vertical acceleration compared with g
Horizontal speed decreasing under drag
Distinguish vertical acceleration from the magnitude of total acceleration
Determine velocity and acceleration directions at a stated point
types.route: Draw the velocity direction, put drag opposite it, and reason about the horizontal and vertical effects separately.
types.spine: A.1.13; A.2 for quantitative force resolution
types.examples: Pack A Q9(c), Q25; O A1.13f, A1.13h; N A1.13b–c; 2025 May SL P1A TZ2 Q3
types.boundary: Claims that acceleration is greater or less than g must specify whether they mean a vertical component or total magnitude.

types.type: Compare ideal and resisted trajectories
subtypes: Range and maximum height
Loss of ascent/descent symmetry
Time of flight for the actual launch and landing conditions
Velocity, impact direction and trajectory steepness
Approach to terminal motion on a sufficiently long fall
types.route: Use the particular launch, landing level and direction of resistance to make qualitative comparisons.
types.examples: Pack A Q25; O A1.13g; N A1.13e; current syllabus
types.boundary: Do not memorize a universal claim that drag always reduces time of flight. The comparison depends on the scenario.

types.type: Determine g or another acceleration from measured motion
subtypes: Fall distance and time
Multi-flash or video position records
Estimate interval velocities and their change
Determine acceleration from an appropriate graph gradient
types.route: Translate measurements into a kinematic relation, use the actual timing intervals, and report acceleration with units.
types.examples: 2024 Nov SL P3 Q2(a); 2018 May SL P3 TZ2 Q1(b); O A1.5d; N A1.9d
types.boundary: These are genuine kinematics data tasks; pendulum-only graph experiments are not used as A.1 evidence.

types.type: Plot, fit or linearise a motion relationship
subtypes: Plot a measured motion trace and draw an appropriate best fit
Choose transformed axes for a supplied kinematic relationship
Interpret gradient and intercept physically
Separate fixed timing/response offsets from speed or braking effects
Use a best-fit gradient or constant gradient to test a motion claim
Interpolation, cautious extrapolation and identifying anomalous points in motion data
types.route: Rearrange the stated model, choose axes and units, fit the data, then interpret parameters and departures from the model.
types.examples: 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ3 Q1(d–e); 2007 Nov P2 A1(e) road-stopping linearisation; O A1.1i
types.boundary: The old road-stopping example is older evidence for a current graph skill, not evidence of a 2025 occurrence.

types.type: Turn periodic marks or detector timing into motion
subtypes: Ticker or regularly timed position marks
A periodic pen trace on an accelerating carrier
Infer an elapsed time from a repeated spatial pattern
Use the time and separation to calculate speed or acceleration
types.route: Establish the clock interval or period, count intervals, then apply the relevant motion equation.
types.examples: 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ1 Q2(a–b); O A1.5f
types.boundary: Determining a period from frequency may add common wave/oscillation knowledge, but the motion calculation remains A.1.

types.type: Correct for the geometry of the measuring arrangement
subtypes: Finite ball diameter and the point triggering a detector
Centre, top or bottom position of an object
Distance travelled during a light-gate interruption
Bias from using the apparatus separation as the travelled distance
types.route: Identify which physical points define each measured event before substituting the distance or time.
types.examples: 2018 May SL P3 TZ2 Q1(a); O A1.5g
types.boundary: In the cited example, the required correction is 654 − 12 = 642 mm; the correct correction depends on the actual geometry.

types.type: Relate image sharpness to exposure or flash duration
subtypes: Maximum exposure for an allowed motion blur
Estimate speed relevant to the image interval
Decide whether the short-exposure constant-speed approximation is adequate
types.route: Relate movement during the exposure to the permitted blur, using a justified local motion estimate.
types.examples: 2024 Nov SL P3 Q2(c); O A1.5e
types.boundary: This subtype is absent from the main teaching-pack examples but present in the database.

types.type: Handle uncertainty and compare measurement with a model
subtypes: Absolute, fractional or percentage uncertainties
Uncertainty in calculated acceleration from measured distances and times
Significant figures and unit conversion
Compare measured g or acceleration with a prediction using uncertainty
Distinguish random variation from a systematic offset
Uncertainty bars, limiting gradients and uncertainty in a gradient-derived parameter
types.route: Use the stated uncertainty rules and model, retain sensible precision, and make the comparison at the uncertainty scale.
types.examples: 2018 May SL P3 TZ2 Q1(b); 2024 Nov SL P3 Q2(b); 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ1 Q2(c)
types.boundary: An explanation using friction or a predicted g sinθ adds A.2; numerical disagreement alone does not identify the cause.

types.type: Evaluate or plan a motion measurement
subtypes: Select useful measured quantities and apparatus
Identify a model assumption such as negligible resistance
Explain departures from predicted motion
Propose a specific improvement to timing, length measurement or data collection
Distinguish a best-fit trend from joining successive noisy points
Choose variables, controls, calibration, measurement range and repeats for a proposed motion investigation
types.route: Connect each limitation or improvement to the quantity measured and its effect on the final motion result.
types.spine: A.1 plus common tools and inquiry
types.examples: 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ1 Q2(c); 2025 Nov SL P1B TZ3 Q1(d–e); current tools/inquiry syllabus
types.boundary: Planning and improvement variants complete the current skills coverage; not every listed variant has a separately verified A.1 past-paper example here.

teaching_taxonomy.membership_status: Vocabulary and examples only; no exhaustive part-to-K-code crosswalk is supplied.

scope_only_review.method: Read each exact own prompt, shared stem, parent context and native scheme text. Resolve current A1 topic demand only; descriptor and image correctness are not certified.

decisions.reason: Resultant displacement and perpendicular displacement components are direct motion-vector demands.
Determine acceleration from a car distance-time graph; direct linear motion-graph interpretation.
The supplied fall relation is used only for uncertainty propagation; no kinematic quantity or model is requested.
Qualitative acceleration-time behaviour during resisted vertical ascent, descent and terminal motion.
Qualitative change of an oblique projectile trajectory with air resistance.
Ordinary ultrasound round-trip distance from the given speed and elapsed time, with no frame transformation.
Explain the constant-deceleration stopping-distance approximation using speed-dependent air resistance.
Determine free-fall acceleration from displacement and elapsed time for release from rest.
Qualitative speed-time curve for a raindrop approaching terminal speed.
Select the speed-time graph for a car with increasing acceleration.
Select the speed-time graph for a car with increasing acceleration.
Select the distance-time graph for resisted fall approaching terminal speed.
Translate a particle acceleration-time graph into instantaneous speed-time behaviour.
Translate a particle acceleration-time graph into instantaneous speed-time behaviour.
Uncertainty propagation through a supplied fall relation is the only requested operation.
Select the speed-time graph during vertical ascent and descent.
Identify the highest point after a bounce from the signed velocity-time graph.
Uncertainty propagation through a supplied fall relation is the only requested operation.
Qualitative speed and acceleration changes before terminal speed.
Qualitative acceleration-time graph for a falling ball with air resistance.
Qualitative acceleration-time graph for resisted fall from rest.
Qualitative speed increase and acceleration decrease during resisted fall.
Qualitative initial acceleration behaviour for an object falling with air resistance.
The requested escape trajectory needs the variation of the gravitational field beyond Venus; no independent A1 relation or supplied motion graph establishes the result.
Translate an ordinary speed-time graph into distance-time behaviour.
Distinguish the downward velocity and upward acceleration after a parachute opens.
Translate an ordinary velocity-time graph into acceleration-time behaviour.
Translate an ordinary velocity-time graph into acceleration-time behaviour.
Velocity direction is inferred from two standing-wave displacement profiles; the direct demand is wave-particle motion.
The requested output is resultant force from motion data; the final taxonomy excludes force-output branches from current A1.
Velocity direction is inferred from two standing-wave displacement profiles; the direct demand is wave-particle motion.
Qualitative acceleration-versus-speed relation during resisted fall.
Elapsed signal time is requested in a moving spacecraft frame and requires relativistic frame reasoning.
Particle velocity is inferred from a travelling wave's spatial displacement profile; direct wave motion demand.
Qualitative changing acceleration of a rising oil droplet from increasing fluid resistance; shared force reasoning does not erase A1.
Qualitative changing acceleration of a rising oil droplet from increasing fluid resistance; shared force reasoning does not erase A1.

analyst_handoff.join_key: source_part_id, identical to current v5 part_id, never a human exam reference alone
analyst_handoff.role_contract: Separate directly assessed descriptors from prerequisite, optional, shared-context and alternative-route descriptors. One row per exact part/descriptor/role/route; preserve multiple direct demands.
analyst_handoff.scope_contract: Explicit current A1 included/excluded/unresolved decision per part. Preserve A1 current SL+HL eligibility; printed historic source level is independent.
analyst_handoff.fine_mapping_gap: Provide the actual part-to-K1–K8 / Kx.y assignments. The September workbook lists examples, not universal mappings. Do not expand an example citation to every member of its older type.

unmatched_literal_evidence.reason: No authored literal evidence survives in the same current v5 field.
No authored literal evidence survives in the same current v5 field.

limitations: This is taxonomy projection, not assessment or crop release clearance.
The blind keep pool is broader than current A1. Final exclusions and split boundaries are retained.
Unsure decisions, split-only membership, missing current evidence and absent IDs remain unmapped.
September K-codes are a teaching synthesis, not a full assignment table; their example references are not expanded into universal memberships.
Secondary family names do not establish prerequisites. No prerequisite or optional demand is inferred.
